nameStory: This microscopic green algae doesn't have a widely-used common name, so scientists simply call it by its scientific name, Micrasterias compereana. The genus name Micrasterias comes from Greek words meaning 'little star,' perfectly describing these tiny organisms that look like intricate, symmetrical stars when viewed under a microscope.
description: Micrasterias compereana is a single-celled green algae that you'll never see with the naked eye - it's only about 0.1 millimeters across! Under a microscope, it looks like a beautiful, flat snowflake or star with intricate lobes and projections radiating from the center. Each cell is perfectly symmetrical, split down the middle into two identical halves. These tiny organisms live in freshwater and are part of a group called desmids, which are known for their stunning geometric shapes.

idTips.label: Symmetrical Star Shape
idTips.description: Under magnification, the cell looks like a perfect six-pointed star with deeply divided lobes that mirror each other exactly across the center line

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely tiny at roughly 100 micrometers (0.1mm) - invisible to naked eye and requires at least 100x magnification to see clearly

idTips.label: Central Constriction
idTips.description: A distinct narrow 'waist' divides the cell into two identical semicircles, like a figure-eight pinched in the middle

idTips.label: Green Color
idTips.description: Bright emerald green throughout, with the color distributed evenly across all the star-like projections

idTips.label: Flat Appearance
idTips.description: Completely flat when viewed from above - no thickness or three-dimensional structure visible under the microscope

habitat: Found in clean, soft freshwater including pristine ponds, quiet lake edges, and slow-moving streams throughout New England's forests and wetlands. Prefers slightly acidic water with low mineral content, often in areas with sphagnum moss or other bog plants. Most commonly discovered in undisturbed woodland pools and the shallow margins of clear mountain lakes.

seasonality.spring: Most active during warming spring months when they reproduce by splitting in half. Best time to find them as populations peak with increased daylight and nutrients.
seasonality.summer: Still present but may be less abundant in very warm weather. Look for them in cooler, shaded water bodies during hot spells.
seasonality.fall: Numbers decline as water temperatures drop and daylight decreases. May still be found in protected spots that stay relatively warm.
seasonality.winter: Largely dormant or present in very low numbers. Some may survive as resistant spores until spring conditions return.

funFact: When Micrasterias reproduces, each half of the cell grows a brand new matching half - like tearing a paper snowflake down the middle and watching each piece magically regrow its missing side to become two identical snowflakes!
confusionNotes: Easily confused with other star-shaped Micrasterias species under the microscope. M. compereana has more deeply divided lobes and a more pronounced central constriction than most relatives. Count the main projections and note the depth of the indentations - this species typically has six primary rays with very deep cuts between them.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'algae,' desmids like Micrasterias are quite different from the stringy green algae most people know. They're actually more closely related to land plants than to seaweeds, and their incredible geometric beauty has made them favorites of microscopy enthusiasts for over 150 years.
compareHints: M. compereana differs from other New England Micrasterias by having particularly deep indentations between its lobes and a more pronounced central constriction. Unlike M. truncata which has blunt-ended projections, M. compereana's rays taper to finer points. It's also typically smaller and more delicately structured than the robust M. americana.
